passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4. Elizabeth Miss, Wednesday.
Observation: Today we rearranged seats so everyone sits with someone new. Thomas refused to move from his window seat. "I always sit here," he said, gripping the desk. His new seat, beside Anjali near the fan, is just as good; last week he told me he wished he could sit near the fan. When I asked what worried him, he said, "I don't know. It's just not my place." He also brings the same lunch every day and takes the same staircase even when the other one is closer.
What I did: I agreed he could try the new seat for two days only, and we'll talk again on Friday. He moved, slowly.

qa.q: Where is Thomas's new seat?
qa.a: His new seat is beside Anjali near the fan.

qa.q: Why did Thomas grip the desk when asked to move?
qa.a: Thomas felt anxious, because the window seat is what he knows and changing felt risky to him. He felt that way even though the new seat was just as good, maybe better.

qa.q: Why was the two-day trial a good idea?
qa.a: It made the change small and safe, with a promise to talk again, so Thomas could test the new seat without feeling he had lost his place for good.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Thomas slowly moves beside her?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a little unsure at first, wondering if he minds sitting there, and may try to make him feel welcome.

grounding: Shows a boy insisting on the same seat, lunch and staircase because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage:
Wednesday
Today Amma made poha instead of upma. I didn't eat it. I always have upma. Irawati ate mine too and said the poha was really nice, with peanuts. Amma said I can't have the same thing every single day of my life. Why not? I like knowing what's coming. Then Papa said we'd take the new road to school because the old one has digging. I cried a bit. The new road had a big tree with parrots, but I didn't look at it much. Tomorrow I want upma, the old road and my same seat. Amma calls me her little upma boy. I don't mind.
Gautam

qa.q: What did Amma make instead of upma?
qa.a: Amma made poha instead of upma.

qa.q: Why did Gautam cry a bit about the new road?
qa.a: He likes knowing what's coming, so a change of route felt risky and upsetting even though the new road had a tree with parrots.

qa.q: How could Amma help Gautam try new things?
qa.a: She could make small changes one at a time, like poha once a week with upma on other days, and talk about something nice on the new road before they go.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about eating the poha?
qa.a: Irawati clearly enjoyed the poha with peanuts and may not understand why the change upset Gautam so much.

grounding: Shows a boy insisting on the same breakfast, route and seat because change feels riskier than what he knows.

passage: In their village near Nashik, a new footbridge had opened across the stream, cutting the walk to school by ten minutes. Salma started using it on the first day. Kiran, nine, kept taking the long path around the field, the one he had walked since class one. "Come on, the bridge is quicker," Salma called from the other side. "I like my way," Kiran said. "I know every stone." In the monsoon the long path turned to mud, and he arrived at school with muddy legs, late twice. Even so, when Salma dared him to try the bridge, he shook his head. "What if it's not as good?"

qa.q: How much time did the new footbridge cut from the walk?
qa.a: The footbridge cut the walk to school by ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Kiran's "What if it's not as good?" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that Kiran feels uneasy about trying something new, so changing feels riskier to him than staying with what he knows, even after the mud and being late twice.

qa.q: What small step could Salma suggest?
qa.a: Salma could suggest trying the bridge just once, walking it together, and going back to the old path the next day if he doesn't like it.

qa.q: How might Salma feel calling from the other side of the bridge?
qa.a: Salma may feel puzzled and a little impatient, but keeps inviting Kiran, which shows real care.

grounding: Shows a boy keeping to his usual long route even when a better one exists, because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage: Every Saturday in Durban, Sami, eight, went to the public library with his big sister Lindiwe, sat at the same corner table by the fish tank, and ate the same jam sandwich at noon. This week, things had moved. The fish tank was now near the windows, and a reading nook with beanbags filled the old corner. Sami froze in the doorway. "Where's my table?" "Look, beanbags!" Lindiwe said. "I want MY table." He sat stiffly at another desk, arms folded, not reading. At noon he refused a new sandwich from the café and ate his jam one. After a while, he crept over to the beanbags, just to look. He sat on one. "It's… okay," he said. Then, quieter, "It's actually squishy."

qa.q: Where had the fish tank been moved to?
qa.a: The fish tank was now near the windows.

qa.q: Why did Sami refuse to enjoy the new beanbags at first?
qa.a: His usual table and routine felt safe and known, so any change felt risky, even though the new nook was fine.

qa.q: What small step helped Sami try the change?
qa.a: He crept over to the beanbags just to look, and then sat on one. Trying a tiny piece of the change let him discover it was okay.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Sami says the beanbag is squishy?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and amused after his stubborn start, and glad he tried it on his own.

grounding: A boy insists on his usual library table and sandwich when things change, then slowly tries the new beanbags.

passage: At the school's summer camp, the dining hall had a new menu: dosa, poha, fruit, or aloo paratha. Manvir, nine, sat at his usual end of table three and asked for aloo paratha, like every day. His friend Rajni said, "Try the dosa, it's crispy." "No. Paratha." Camp teacher Jasleen ma'am noticed that Manvir also walked the long way to the pool, past the kitchen, though a new garden path was shorter. "Why that way?" she asked. He shrugged. "It's my way." On Friday, Rajni dared him to walk the garden path with her. He went slowly, looking around. Butterflies circled the hibiscus. "Hm," he said. "Same pool at the end." The next morning he tried half a dosa.

qa.q: Where was Manvir's usual seat?
qa.a: At the end of table three.

qa.q: Why did Manvir keep walking the long way to the pool?
qa.a: The usual way felt safe because he knew it, and trying the new path felt like a risk, even though it was shorter and fine.

qa.q: What helped Manvir try something new, and what could adults learn from it?
qa.a: Rajni's friendly dare to walk the garden path together. A small, shared first try made the change feel safe, which led him to taste half a dosa too.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when Manvir tries half a dosa?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased, as her patient invitations finally helped her friend try something new.

grounding: At summer camp, a boy sticks to the same seat, breakfast and route until a friend helps him try a new path.
